title: Apply attention-based models to other tasks
description: The authors are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks beyond sequence transduction.
canonical_description: need to apply attention-based models to a broader range of tasks

evidence.anchor: plan to apply them to other tasks
evidence.quote: We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks.

verdict.reasoning: Two direct_solution papers together cover the gap convincingly: Music Transformer applies attention-based models to symbolic music generation (unconditional generation, motif continuation, seq2seq harmonization) — a task firmly outside sequence transduction — and RCCT applies Vision Transformers to unsupervised domain adaptation for image classification, showing state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks. Both are explicit, concrete demonstrations of attention models succeeding on tasks beyond the original domain. The partial solutions (DiNA for vision tasks, NSA for image captioning/video captioning/MT/VQA) add further weight. The gap is broad ("apply to other tasks") and does not require exhaustive coverage of every possible domain — these papers demonstrate the feasibility the gap sought. The confidence is high because the evidence is direct and the papers are squarely on-point.

paper.title: Music Transformer
paper.abstract: Music relies heavily on repetition to build structure and meaning. Self-reference occurs on multiple timescales, from motifs to phrases to reusing of entire sections of music, such as in pieces with ABA structure. The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), a sequence model based on self-attention, has achieved compelling results in many generation tasks that require maintaining long-range coherence. This suggests that self-attention might also be well-suited to modeling music. In musical composition and performance, however, relative timing is critically important. Existing approaches for representing relative positional information in the Transformer modulate attention based on pairwise distance (Shaw et al., 2018). This is impractical for long sequences such as musical compositions since their memory complexity for intermediate relative information is quadratic in the sequence length. We propose an algorithm that reduces their intermediate memory requirement to linear in the sequence length. This enables us to demonstrate that a Transformer with our modified relative attention mechanism can generate minute-long compositions (thousands of steps, four times the length modeled in Oore et al., 2018) with compelling structure, generate continuations that coherently elaborate on a given motif, and in a seq2seq setup generate accompaniments conditioned on melodies. We evaluate the Transformer with our relative attention mechanism on two datasets, JSB Chorales and Piano-e-Competition, and obtain state-of-the-art results on the latter.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper applies the Transformer (an attention-based model) to symbolic music generation, a task well beyond the original sequence transduction domain. It demonstrates the Transformer's effectiveness on three music tasks: unconditional generation of minute-long piano performances, continuation/elaboration of a given motif, and seq2seq harmonization (generating accompaniments conditioned on melodies). The paper also introduces a memory-efficient implementation of relative attention that makes it practical to apply Transformers to long musical sequences (thousands of steps).
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of applying attention-based models to other tasks beyond sequence transduction — it successfully applies the Transformer to music generation. However, the gap is broadly stated ("other tasks"), and this paper only covers music generation tasks. Many other domains (e.g., video, robotics, scientific data, etc.) remain unexplored by this specific paper, but that is inherent to the broadness of the original gap statement. The paper itself acknowledges this in its conclusion: "Our memory-efficient implementation enables the application of relative attention to much longer sequences such as long texts or even audio waveforms, which significantly broadens the range of problems to which it could be applied."
evidence_snippets: We show the first successful use of Transformers in generating music that exhibits long-term structure.
In a seq2seq setup, Transformers can generate accompaniments conditioned on melodies, enabling users to interact with the model.

Our memory-efficient implementation enables the application of relative attention to much longer sequences such as long texts or even audio waveforms, which significantly broadens the range of problems to which it could be applied.

paper.title: Robust Core-Periphery Constrained Transformer for Domain Adaptation
paper.abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to learn transferable representation across domains. Recently a few UDA works have successfully applied Transformer-based methods and achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) results. However, it remains challenging when there exists a large domain gap between the source and target domain. Inspired by humans' exceptional transferability abilities to adapt knowledge from familiar to uncharted domains, we try to apply the universally existing organizational structure in the human functional brain networks, i.e., the core-periphery principle to design the Transformer and improve its UDA performance. In this paper, we propose a novel brain-inspired robust core-periphery constrained transformer (RCCT) for unsupervised domain adaptation, which brings a large margin of performance improvement on various datasets. Specifically, in RCCT, the self-attention operation across image patches is rescheduled by an adaptively learned weighted graph with the Core-Periphery structure (CP graph), where the information communication and exchange between images patches are manipulated and controlled by the connection strength, i.e., edge weight of the learned weighted CP graph. Besides, since the data in domain adaptation tasks can be noisy, to improve the model robustness, we intentionally add perturbations to the patches in the latent space to ensure generating robust learned weighted core-periphery graphs. Extensive evaluations are conducted on several widely tested UDA benchmarks. Our proposed RCCT consistently performs best compared to existing works, including 88.3\% on Office-Home, 95.0\% on Office-31, 90.7\% on VisDA-2017, and 46.0\% on DomainNet.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper applies attention-based models (specifically Vision Transformers with a novel core-periphery constrained self-attention mechanism) to the task of unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for image classification. The authors propose RCCT, which instills a brain-inspired core-periphery structure into the Transformer's self-attention to improve domain adaptation performance. The paper demonstrates state-of-the-art results on multiple UDA benchmarks (Office-Home, Office-31, VisDA-2017, DomainNet), showing that attention-based models can be successfully applied to domain adaptation tasks beyond the original sequence transduction setting.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is fully addressed by this paper. The paper explicitly applies attention-based models (Transformers) to a new task (unsupervised domain adaptation) beyond sequence transduction, which is exactly what the gap calls for. The paper demonstrates this application with extensive experiments and strong results. No part of the gap remains open — the paper is a concrete instantiation of applying attention-based models to another task.
evidence_snippets: Recently, the self-attention mechanism and its variant vision transformer (ViT) have received growing interest in the vision community. ... Due to the superiority of the self-attention mechanism in global content capture, ViT and its variants have obtained impressive performance on kinds of vision tasks, such as image classification, video understanding, object detection, and content segmentation.

In this paper, we propose a novel brain-inspired robust core-periphery constrained transformer (RCCT) for unsupervised domain adaptation, which brings a large margin of performance improvement on various datasets.

RCCT is one of the pioneers in exploring the vision transformer for unsupervised domain adaptation. Also, our proposed RCCT demonstrates that the brain-inspired vision transformer has its superiority by showing SOTA results on the widely tested datasets, including 88.3% on Office-Home, 95.0% on Office-31, 90.7% on VisDA-2017 and 46.0% on DomainNet.

paper.title: Dilated Neighborhood Attention Transformer
paper.abstract: Transformers are quickly becoming one of the most heavily applied deep learning architectures across modalities, domains, and tasks. In vision, on top of ongoing efforts into plain transformers, hierarchical transformers have also gained significant attention, thanks to their performance and easy integration into existing frameworks. These models typically employ localized attention mechanisms, such as the sliding-window Neighborhood Attention (NA) or Swin Transformer's Shifted Window Self Attention. While effective at reducing self attention's quadratic complexity, local attention weakens two of the most desirable properties of self attention: long range inter-dependency modeling, and global receptive field. In this paper, we introduce Dilated Neighborhood Attention (DiNA), a natural, flexible and efficient extension to NA that can capture more global context and expand receptive fields exponentially at no additional cost. NA's local attention and DiNA's sparse global attention complement each other, and therefore we introduce Dilated Neighborhood Attention Transformer (DiNAT), a new hierarchical vision transformer built upon both. DiNAT variants enjoy significant improvements over strong baselines such as NAT, Swin, and ConvNeXt. Our large model is faster and ahead of its Swin counterpart by 1.6% box AP in COCO object detection, 1.4% mask AP in COCO instance segmentation, and 1.4% mIoU in ADE20K semantic segmentation. Paired with new frameworks, our large variant is the new state of the art panoptic segmentation model on COCO (58.5 PQ) and ADE20K (49.4 PQ), and instance segmentation model on Cityscapes (45.1 AP) and ADE20K (35.4 AP) (no extra data). It also matches the state of the art specialized semantic segmentation models on ADE20K (58.1 mIoU), and ranks second on Cityscapes (84.5 mIoU) (no extra data).

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper introduces Dilated Neighborhood Attention (DiNA) and the DiNAT vision transformer, applying attention-based models to a range of computer vision tasks including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, semantic segmentation, and panoptic segmentation. This demonstrates that attention-based models can be successfully applied to vision tasks beyond the original sequence transduction domain. The paper also open-sources the CUDA extension to support further research in this direction.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap calls for applying attention-based models to "other tasks" broadly — beyond sequence transduction. While this paper successfully applies attention to vision tasks, it does not provide a general framework or methodology for applying attention-based models to arbitrary new tasks or domains (e.g., speech, reinforcement learning, graph data, scientific computing, etc.). The paper focuses specifically on a particular attention variant (dilated neighborhood attention) for vision, rather than addressing how to systematically adapt attention mechanisms to new problem domains in general.
evidence_snippets: Transformers are quickly becoming one of the most heavily applied deep learning architectures across modalities, domains, and tasks.
To support and encourage research in this direction, in vision and beyond, we open-source our project at: https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Neighborhood-Attention-Transformer.
We believe that combinations of NA and DiNA will be able to empower various models in vision and beyond, wherever locality and global context matter.

paper.title: Mask-Attention-Free Transformer for 3D Instance Segmentation
paper.abstract: Recently, transformer-based methods have dominated 3D instance segmentation, where mask attention is commonly involved. Specifically, object queries are guided by the initial instance masks in the first cross-attention, and then iteratively refine themselves in a similar manner. However, we observe that the mask-attention pipeline usually leads to slow convergence due to low-recall initial instance masks. Therefore, we abandon the mask attention design and resort to an auxiliary center regression task instead. Through center regression, we effectively overcome the low-recall issue and perform cross-attention by imposing positional prior. To reach this goal, we develop a series of position-aware designs. First, we learn a spatial distribution of 3D locations as the initial position queries. They spread over the 3D space densely, and thus can easily capture the objects in a scene with a high recall. Moreover, we present relative position encoding for the cross-attention and iterative refinement for more accurate position queries. Experiments show that our approach converges 4x faster than existing work, sets a new state of the art on ScanNetv2 3D instance segmentation benchmark, and also demonstrates superior performance across various datasets. Code and models are available at https://github.com/dvlab-research/Mask-Attention-Free-Transformer.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes a mask-attention-free transformer for 3D instance segmentation. It replaces the standard mask-attention mechanism with an auxiliary center regression task and position-aware designs (learnable position queries, relative position encoding, iterative refinement) to accelerate convergence and improve performance on 3D instance segmentation benchmarks. This is a technical improvement within an already-established application of transformers to 3D vision, not an exploration of applying attention-based models to new tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap calls for applying attention-based models to tasks beyond sequence transduction — i.e., exploring whether the Transformer architecture generalizes to other domains. This paper does not address that question: it operates entirely within the already-established paradigm of applying transformers to 3D vision tasks (which was well-explored by prior work such as Mask3D and SPFormer). The gap of systematically exploring attention-based models for novel task domains, or demonstrating their applicability to tasks where they haven't been tried before, remains entirely open.

paper.title: Normalized and Geometry-Aware Self-Attention Network for Image Captioning
paper.abstract: Self-attention (SA) network has shown profound value in image captioning. In this paper, we improve SA from two aspects to promote the performance of image captioning. First, we propose Normalized Self-Attention (NSA), a reparameterization of SA that brings the benefits of normalization inside SA. While normalization is previously only applied outside SA, we introduce a novel normalization method and demonstrate that it is both possible and beneficial to perform it on the hidden activations inside SA. Second, to compensate for the major limit of Transformer that it fails to model the geometry structure of the input objects, we propose a class of Geometry-aware Self-Attention (GSA) that extends SA to explicitly and efficiently consider the relative geometry relations between the objects in the image. To construct our image captioning model, we combine the two modules and apply it to the vanilla self-attention network. We extensively evaluate our proposals on MS-COCO image captioning dataset and superior results are achieved when comparing to state-of-the-art approaches. Further experiments on three challenging tasks, i.e. video captioning, machine translation, and visual question answering, show the generality of our methods.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes two improvements to self-attention (Normalized Self-Attention and Geometry-aware Self-Attention) and applies them primarily to image captioning, achieving state-of-the-art results on MS-COCO. To demonstrate generality, the authors also test their methods on three additional tasks: video captioning (VATEX dataset), machine translation (WMT 2014 En-De), and visual question answering (VQA-v2). On all tasks, replacing vanilla self-attention with their proposed modules yields improvements over strong baselines.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap calls for applying attention-based models to a broad range of tasks beyond sequence transduction. While this paper tests on four tasks (image captioning, video captioning, MT, VQA), the primary focus is on improving self-attention rather than exploring fundamentally new task domains. The paper does not explore tasks outside vision-and-language or translation — for example, tasks in reinforcement learning, graph-structured data, speech/audio processing, time-series forecasting, or other domains where attention models could be applied. The gap about broadly applying attention-based models to many diverse tasks remains largely open.
evidence_snippets: Further experiments on three challenging tasks, \ie video captioning, machine translation, and visual question answering, show the generality of our methods.
We further investigate the effectiveness and generality of our methods on Video Captioning (VC), Machine Translation (MT), and Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks.
On all tasks, simply replacing the vanilla SA module with our proposed methods provides solid improvements over strong baselines.
